evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: The relative expression levels of GLI1 mRNA in the cerebral cortex of ferrets were significantly higher than those of mice (ferret, 0.58 ± 0.16; mouse, 0.30 ± 0.08; p=0.048).
source: Our quantification showed that the relative expression levels of GLI1 mRNA in the cerebral cortex of ferrets were significantly higher than those of mice (ferret, 0.58 ± 0.16; mouse, 0.30 ± 0.08; p=0.048; Student's t-test) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative RT-PCR analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Shh signaling is activated in neural progenitors much more in ferrets than in mice.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Shh signaling is activated in neural progenitors much more in ferrets than in mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the GLI1 expression data comparing ferrets and mice.

claim: Shh protein levels were much higher in ferrets than in mice in the cerebral cortex.
source: Interestingly, Shh protein levels were much higher in ferrets than in mice (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Protein levels of Shh in cerebella were similar in both ferrets and mice.
source: Protein levels of Shh in cerebella were similar in both species (Figure 6H), indicating that both ferret Shh and mouse Shh are recognized with similar affinity by this anti-Shh antibody.
evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Both ferret Shh and mouse Shh are recognized with similar affinity by the anti-Shh antibody.
source: Protein levels of Shh in cerebella were similar in both species (Figure 6H), indicating that both ferret Shh and mouse Shh are recognized with similar affinity by this anti-Shh antibody.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar Shh levels in cerebella of both species.

claim: Shh protein levels in the cerebral cortex of ferrets were significantly higher than those in mice (mouse, 0.10 ± 0.01; ferret, 0.32 ± 0.05; p=0.002).
source: Our quantification showed that Shh protein levels in the cerebral cortex of ferrets were significantly higher than those in mice (mouse, 0.10 ± 0.01; ferret, 0.32 ± 0.05; p=0.002; Student's t-test) (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is based on quantitative western blotting analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Shh ligand is more abundant in the cerebral cortex of ferrets than in that of mice.
source: Thus, these results indicate that Shh ligand is more abundant in the cerebral cortex of ferrets than in that of mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the western blotting data.

claim: GLI1 mRNA levels in single HOPX-positive cells in the SVZ were significantly higher in ferrets than in mice (mouse, 0.18 ± 0.05; ferret, 0.39 ± 0.06; p=0.04).
source: Consistent with this conclusion, GLI1 mRNA levels in single HOPX-positive cells in the SVZ were significantly higher in ferrets than in mice (mouse, 0.18 ± 0.05; ferret, 0.39 ± 0.06; p=0.04; Student's t-test) (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Highly activated Shh signaling in the gyrencephalic mammals underlies the expansion of HOPX-positive oRG cells and the acquisition of cortical folds.
source: It seems plausible that highly activated Shh signaling in the gyrencephalic mammals underlies the expansion of HOPX-positive oRG cells and the acquisition of cortical folds.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Shh signaling levels and cortical folding.

claim: HOPX-positive oRG cells predominantly accumulated in prospective gyral regions compared with HOPX-negative oRG cells.
source: In this study, we revealed that HOPX-positive oRG cells predominantly accumulated in prospective gyral regions compared with HOPX-negative oRG cells.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the distribution analysis.

claim: HOPX-positive oRG cells had higher Shh signaling activity than HOPX-negative oRG cells.
source: HOPX-positive oRG cells had higher Shh signaling activity and lower differentiation rates than HOPX-negative oRG cells.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the GLI1 expression analysis.

claim: HOPX-positive oRG cells had lower differentiation rates than HOPX-negative oRG cells.
source: HOPX-positive oRG cells had higher Shh signaling activity and lower differentiation rates than HOPX-negative oRG cells.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the EdU labeling experiments.

claim: HOPX-positive oRG cells were selectively increased by the activation of Shh signaling.
source: Furthermore, HOPX-positive oRG cells were selectively increased by the activation of Shh signaling.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the Shh-N experiments.

claim: HOPX-positive and HOPX-negative oRG cells have distinct cellular properties.
source: These several lines of evidence support the idea that HOPX-positive and HOPX-negative oRG cells have distinct cellular properties and that HOPX-positive oRG cells mediate cortical folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple differences observed between the two cell types.

claim: HOPX-positive oRG cells mediate cortical folding.
source: These several lines of evidence support the idea that HOPX-positive and HOPX-negative oRG cells have distinct cellular properties and that HOPX-positive oRG cells mediate cortical folding.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between HOPX-positive oRG cells and cortical folding.

claim: The expansion of HOPX-positive oRG cells is a key feature of gyrencephalic brains.
source: The expansion of HOPX-positive oRG cells seems to be a key feature of gyrencephalic brains.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data between gyrencephalic and lissencephalic species.

claim: The proliferation of oRG cells was regulated by FGF signaling in vivo.
source: Our previous study demonstrated that the proliferation of oRG cells was regulated by FGF signaling in vivo. When a dominant-negative form of FGF receptor 3 was introduced into the ferret cerebral cortex by IUE, the proliferation of oRG cells was suppressed (Matsumoto et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: When a dominant-negative form of FGF receptor 3 was introduced into the ferret cerebral cortex by IUE, the proliferation of oRG cells was suppressed.
source: Our previous study demonstrated that the proliferation of oRG cells was regulated by FGF signaling in vivo. When a dominant-negative form of FGF receptor 3 was introduced into the ferret cerebral cortex by IUE, the proliferation of oRG cells was suppressed (Matsumoto et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Shh signaling suppresses the differentiation of HOPX-positive oRG cells and promotes their self-renewal in the developing ferret cerebral cortex.
source: Our findings clearly indicate that Shh signaling suppresses the differentiation of HOPX-positive oRG cells and promotes their self-renewal in the developing ferret cerebral cortex.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from the HhipΔC22 and EdU experiments.

claim: Shh signaling induces the expression of Cdk6 in the developing vertebrate limb.
source: Previously, it was reported that Shh signaling induces the expression of Cdk6 in the developing vertebrate limb (McGlinn et al., 2005) and that Cdk6 inhibits the differentiation of myeloid progenitors (Fujimoto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cdk6 inhibits the differentiation of myeloid progenitors.
source: Previously, it was reported that Shh signaling induces the expression of Cdk6 in the developing vertebrate limb (McGlinn et al., 2005) and that Cdk6 inhibits the differentiation of myeloid progenitors (Fujimoto et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Shh signaling could suppress the differentiation of oRG cells through Cdk6.
source: Therefore, Shh signaling could suppress the differentiation of oRG cells through Cdk6.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known roles of Shh and Cdk6.

claim: Inhibition of Notch, integrin and STAT signaling resulted in a reduced number of oRG cells in vitro.
source: Other in vitro studies demonstrated that inhibition of Notch, integrin and STAT signaling resulted in a reduced number of oRG cells (Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010; Pollen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Constitutive activation of Shh signaling in neural progenitors induced cortical folds in the medial regions of the cerebral cortex in transgenic mice.
source: Previous pioneering studies using transgenic mice reported that constitutive activation of Shh signaling in neural progenitors induced cortical folds in the medial regions of the cerebral cortex (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Transgenic mice with constitutive activation of Shh signaling did not show obvious cortical folding in most of the cerebral cortex.
source: These transgenic mice, however, did not show obvious cortical folding in most of the cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is based on the description of previous transgenic mouse studies.

claim: Shh signaling plays a crucial role in cortical folding in the ferret cerebral cortex.
source: Our gain- and loss-of-function in vivo experiments using ferret IUE clearly indicate that Shh signaling plays a crucial role in cortical folding in the ferret cerebral cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the gain- and loss-of-function experiments.

claim: Shh activity regulates synaptic connections in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: For example, it was previously reported that Shh activity regulates synaptic connections in the mouse cerebral cortex (Harwell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Shh signaling promotes myelination in the developing mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Another recent study suggested that Shh signaling promotes myelination in the developing mouse cerebral cortex (Zakaria et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Shh signaling was more highly activated in the human cerebral cortex than in the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: In agreement with this finding, a previous study demonstrated that Shh signaling was more highly activated in the human cerebral cortex than in the mouse cerebral cortex (Heng et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Shh signaling is commonly activated in the gyrencephalic cerebral cortex of various animal species.
source: It is thus conceivable that Shh signaling is commonly activated in the gyrencephalic cerebral cortex of various animal species.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data across species.

claim: High Shh signaling activity is one of the important changes in the evolution of the mammalian brain.
source: High Shh signaling activity seems to be one of the important changes in the evolution of the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between Shh signaling and gyrencephaly.

claim: An increase in the diversity of neural progenitor subtypes is associated with the appearance of cortical folding during evolution.
source: An increase in the diversity of neural progenitor subtypes is associated with the appearance of cortical folding during evolution (Dehay et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Kriegstein et al., 2006; Molnár et al., 2006; Rakic, 2009; Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The developing cerebral cortex of the lissencephalic mouse brain contains two germinal layers, the ventricular zone (VZ) and the subventricular zone (SVZ).
source: The developing cerebral cortex of the lissencephalic mouse brain contains two germinal layers, the ventricular zone (VZ) and the subventricular zone (SVZ), which comprise radial glial cells (RG cells, also known as apical progenitors/ventricular RG cells/apical RG cells) and intermediate progenitor (IP) cells, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse brain development.

claim: The SVZ of humans, monkeys and ferrets is radially expanded and further subdivided into the inner SVZ (ISVZ) and the outer SVZ (OSVZ).
source: The SVZ of humans, monkeys and ferrets is radially expanded and further subdivided into the inner SVZ (ISVZ) and the outer SVZ (OSVZ), which contains abundant outer radial glial cells (oRG cells, also known as OSVZ RG cells/basal RG cells/intermediate RG cells/translocating RG cells).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gyrencephalic brain development.

claim: The OSVZ contains abundant outer radial glial cells (oRG cells).
source: The SVZ of humans, monkeys and ferrets is radially expanded and further subdivided into the inner SVZ (ISVZ) and the outer SVZ (OSVZ), which contains abundant outer radial glial cells (oRG cells, also known as OSVZ RG cells/basal RG cells/intermediate RG cells/translocating RG cells).
evidence: This is established knowledge about gyrencephalic brain development.

claim: The acquisition of cortical folds during evolution resulted from increased numbers and diversity of neural progenitors.
source: Although it has been proposed that the acquisition of cortical folds during evolution resulted from increased numbers and diversity of neural progenitors (Dehay et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2016; Florio and Huttner, 2014; Kriegstein et al., 2006; Molnár et al., 2006; Rakic, 2009; Sun and Hevner, 2014), it has been difficult to test this proposal experimentally in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Not all oRG cells express HOPX in the human cerebral cortex.
source: Interestingly, a previous study showed that not all oRG cells express HOPX in the human cerebral cortex (Thomsen et al., 2016), raising the possibility that oRG cells consist of multiple subtypes of neural progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: HOPX was also reported to be expressed in oRG cells of other gyrencephalic animals such as monkeys and ferrets.
source: HOPX was also reported to be expressed in oRG cells of other gyrencephalic animals such as monkeys and ferrets (Johnson et al., 2018; Pollen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortical folding is believed to underlie the acquisition of higher brain functions during development and evolution.
source: Cortical folding is believed to underlie the acquisition of higher brain functions during development and evolution (Florio and Huttner, 2014; Llinares-Benadero and Borrell, 2019; Lui et al., 2011; Sun and Hevner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Malformations of cortical folds are often associated with intellectual disabilities, epilepsy and diseases such as schizophrenia and autism.
source: Consistent with this proposition, malformations of cortical folds are often associated with intellectual disabilities, epilepsy and diseases such as schizophrenia and autism (Fernández et al., 2016; Ross and Walsh, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reductions in SVZ progenitors resulted in the impairment of cortical folding in the naturally gyrencephalic ferret in vivo.
source: Using these techniques, we showed that reductions in SVZ progenitors resulted in the impairment of cortical folding in the naturally gyrencephalic ferret in vivo (Matsumoto et al., 2017b; Toda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Increased SVZ progenitors in the lissencephalic mouse cerebral cortex was not sufficient for inducing de novo formation of cortical folds.
source: Although these data indicate the importance of SVZ progenitors for cortical folding, increased SVZ progenitors in the lissencephalic mouse cerebral cortex was not sufficient for inducing de novo formation of cortical folds (Nonaka-Kinoshita et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.
